source_text: Quando autem stamus ad orationem, fratres dilectissimi, inuigilare et incumbere ad preces toto corde debemus. cogitatio omnis carnalis et saecularis abscedat nec quicquam animus quam id solum cogitet quod precatur. ideo et sacerdos ante orationem i praefatione praemissa parat fratrum mentes dicendo: susum corda, ut dum respondet plebs: habemus ad Dominum, admoneatur nihil aliud se quam Dominum cogitare debere. cludatur contra aduersarium pectus et soli Deo pateat nec ad se adire hostem Dei tempore orationis patiatur. obrepit enim frequenter et penetrat et subtiliter fallens preces nostras a Deo auocat, ut aliud habeamus in corde, aliud in uoce, quando intentione sincera Dominum non uocis sonus sed animus et sensus debeat orare. quae autem segnitia est abalienari et capi ineptis cogitationibus et profanis, cum Dominum deprecaris, quasi sit aliud quod magis debeas cogitare quam quod cum Deo loqueris. quomodo audiri te a Deo postulas, cum te ipse non audias? uis esse Dominum memorem tui cum rogas, quando tui memor ipse non sis ? hoc est ab hoste in totum non cauere, hoc est, quando oras Deum, maiestatem Dei neglegentia orationis offendere, hoc est uigilare oculis et corde dormire, cum debeat christianus et cum dormit oculis corde uigilare, sicut scriptum est ex persona ecclesiae loquentis in Cantico cantiorum: ego dormio et cor meum uigilat. quapropter sollicite et caute apostolus admonet dicens: instate orationi uigilantes in ea, docens scilicet et ostendens eos inpetrare quod postulant de Deo posse, quos Deus uideat in oratione uigilare.
orientation: Cyprian is addressing his fellow Christians about the inner disposition required when they stand to pray.
pass_a_gloss: But when we stand for prayer, most beloved brothers, we ought to watch and press upon prayers with the whole heart. Let every carnal and worldly thought depart, and let the mind think nothing other than that alone which it prays. Therefore also the priest before the prayer, with a preface sent ahead, prepares the minds of the brothers by saying: lift up your hearts, so that while the people responds: we have them to the Lord, it may be admonished that it ought to think nothing other than the Lord. Let the breast be shut against the adversary and be open to God alone, and let it not allow the enemy of God to approach it at the time of prayer. For he creeps in frequently and penetrates and, subtly deceiving, calls our prayers away from God, so that we have one thing in the heart, another in the voice, when with sincere intention not the sound of the voice but the mind and the understanding ought to pray to the Lord. But what sloth is it to be alienated and seized by foolish and profane thoughts, when you entreat the Lord, as if there were something else that you ought to think about more than that which you speak with God. How do you ask that you be heard by God, when you yourself do not hear yourself? Do you wish the Lord to be mindful of you when you ask, when you yourself are not mindful of yourself? This is not to beware of the enemy at all, this is, when you pray to God, to offend the majesty of God by the negligence of prayer, this is to watch with the eyes and to sleep with the heart, when a Christian ought even when he sleeps with the eyes to watch with the heart, as it is written from the person of the church speaking in the Song of Songs: I sleep and my heart watches. Wherefore the apostle carefully and cautiously admonishes, saying: be constant in prayer, watching in it, teaching of course and showing that those whom God sees watching in prayer are able to obtain what they ask from God.

choices.why: Cyprian's standard address to his fellow Christians; 'dilectissimi' is superlative, so 'most beloved' preserves the force.
This is the liturgical dialogue; 'susum' is the Old Latin form of 'sursum', and the phrase is the traditional English rendering of the Sursum Corda.

choices.english: we have them to the Lord
choices.why: The people's response in the liturgical dialogue; the literal sense is 'we have them (our hearts) to the Lord', preserving the Old Latin construction with 'ad'.
rejected: we lift them up to the Lord
we have them unto the Lord

choices.why: The phrase identifies the adversary as God's enemy; the literal rendering keeps the genitive relation explicit.
'Intentione' is ablative of manner; 'sincera' means pure, genuine, so 'sincere intention' preserves the moral quality Cyprian emphasizes.

choices.english: be constant in prayer, watching in it
choices.why: This is a Pauline citation; 'instate' is a plural imperative meaning 'persist, be constant', and 'uigilantes in ea' is a participle phrase modifying the command.
rejected: persist in prayer, being watchful in it
continue in prayer, watching in it

bible_refs.note: ego dormio et cor meum uigilat

pass_b_english: But when we stand to pray, most beloved brothers, we must be watchful and press our whole heart into our prayers. Every carnal and worldly thought must leave, and the mind must think of nothing except the very thing it is praying for. That is why the priest, before the prayer, prepares the minds of the brothers with a preface, saying: “Lift up your hearts,” so that when the people answer, “We have them to the Lord,” they are reminded that they ought to think of nothing but the Lord. Let the breast be shut against the adversary and open to God alone, and let it not allow the enemy of God to approach it during the time of prayer. For he often creeps in and penetrates, and by subtle deceit calls our prayers away from God, so that we have one thing in the heart and another on the lips, when it is not the sound of the voice but the mind and understanding that ought to pray to the Lord with sincere intention. What sloth it is to be carried off and seized by foolish and profane thoughts when you are entreating the Lord, as if there were something else you ought to think about more than the fact that you are speaking with God. How do you ask God to hear you when you do not hear yourself? Do you want the Lord to remember you when you ask, when you yourself are not mindful of yourself? This is failing to guard against the enemy at all; this is offending the majesty of God by careless prayer when you pray to God; this is being awake with the eyes and asleep in the heart, when a Christian ought to be awake in heart even while sleeping with the eyes, as it is written from the person of the church speaking in the Song of Songs: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song of Songs 5:2). Therefore the apostle carefully and cautiously warns, saying: “Be constant in prayer, watching in it” (Colossians 4:2), teaching and showing that those whom God sees watching in prayer are able to obtain from God what they ask.

problems.why: The Latin matches Romans 12:12 ("instantes in oratione, vigilantes"), not Colossians 4:2 ("orationi vigilantes").
problems.ruling: Latin 'instate orationi uigilantes in ea' matches Romans 12:12, not Colossians 4:2; wrong scripture reference misleads reader.

fixed: Changed 'Colossians 4:2' to 'Romans 12:12': the Latin 'instate orationi uigilantes in ea' matches Romans 12:12, not Colossians 4:2.

problems.quote: when you yourself are not mindful of yourself
problems.source_quote: quando tui memor ipse non sis
problems.why: "tui" refers to God, not oneself; the parallel is "Dominum memorem tui" (Lord mindful of you).
problems.fix: when you yourself are not mindful of him
problems.ruling: 'tui memor ipse non sis' parallels 'Dominum memorem tui'; 'tui' = 'you,' not 'yourself.' Translation says 'mindful of yourself,' missing the contrast.

fixed: Corrected 'when you yourself are not mindful of yourself' to 'when you yourself are not mindful of him': source 'quando tui memor ipse non sis' has 'tui' as objective genitive referring to God, paralleling 'Dominum memorem tui' (the Lord mindful of you).

problems.fix: when you yourself are not mindful of yourself?
problems.ruling: tui memor = mindful of yourself, not 'of him'; ipsum/illum would mean 'of him'.

fixed: Source 'quando tui memor ipse non sis' uses 'tui' (of yourself), so the English should read 'not mindful of yourself', not 'of him'.

problems.quote: “Be constant in prayer, watching in it” (Romans 12:12)
problems.why: The quoted line, including “watching in it,” is Colossians 4:2. Romans 12:12 has only “be constant in prayer.”
problems.fix: “Be constant in prayer, watching in it” (Colossians 4:2)
problems.ruling: Source 'instate orationi uigilantes in ea' is Colossians 4:2 (Vulgate: 'Orationi instate, vigilantes in ea'); Romans 12:12 lacks 'watching in it', so citation is wrong.

last_rejected.quote: We have them to the Lord
last_rejected.why: "Them" is wrong: "ad Dominum" means "toward the Lord," not "to the Lord" as possession. The response means "We hold/lift them up toward the Lord."
last_rejected.fix: "We lift them up to the Lord" or "We hold them toward the Lord"
last_rejected.ruling: 'To the Lord' is standard liturgical rendering of 'ad Dominum'; 'them' correctly supplies 'hearts' (corda). Not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: when you yourself are not mindful of yourself
last_rejected.source_quote: quando tui memor ipse non sis
last_rejected.why: "Of yourself" is wrong: "tui" is genitive of "tu," meaning "of you" (i.e., God remembering you), not reflexive. The contrast is between God remembering you and you not remembering God/your prayer.
last_rejected.fix: when you yourself are not mindful of him
last_rejected.ruling: 'tui memor' = 'mindful of yourself'; 'ipse' reinforces reflexive. Translation correctly captures the self-contrast. Not wrong.

last_rejected.quote: those whom God sees watching in prayer are able to obtain from God what they ask
last_rejected.source_quote: eos inpetrare quod postulant de Deo posse, quos Deus uideat in oratione uigilare
last_rejected.why: Wrong agency: the Latin says God sees them watching, and therefore they are able to obtain; the English makes "those whom God sees" the subject of "are able," but obscures that God's seeing enables the obtaining.
last_rejected.fix: that those are able to obtain from God what they ask, whom God sees watching in prayer
last_rejected.ruling: English accurately conveys 'eos...posse...quos Deus uideat': those whom God sees watching can obtain. Causal sense is preserved.
